source_text: So, this is probably good enough for a start, we're not trying to be fully scientific about it, and having a few shaky rows or broken rules makes it even better as a "live" project.  What starts to become interesting is what actual customer or client problems any of this might solve for anyone.  Asking that could explain why some of the verbs are more interesting than others.  For example, for me personally, in order to start to get the War Machine to work in a reasonable way, I needed to create a Lean specification at the node level, and then work hard to produce a run-time-behaviour model that matched how it was supposed to operate.  We're still in the process of validating it, and even when it works, I don't know if it will be great for anything as a computational tool.  But as a model of the way people and organisations work, it seems like a great schematic.  (Presumably whatever list of verbs we find or come up with can be fitted to the PBASE and R-number outlines that describe War Machine.)  Going back to my question, a given company out there in middle America or wherever is going to be turning to AI/tech/agents/etc. to solve some actual problem for themselves or their clients.  And in principle having a model of how the space works should allow us to help them solve it faster or better.  Now, some problems are totally "human" problems, e.g. managers that don't listen to their employees won't be "solved" with Elephant-2000 methods for example.

reply_text:
㊥ (gist) I've added this to the mission as §3.1 (commit `7a15814`). It covers your turn, a test for telling human problems from ones tooling can help with, and a first mapping of the triples onto the War Machine's R-nodes.

🈖 ("totally "human" problems") The SVO form gives a fairly clean way to separate the two. A tool can only change the *via* column, which is how faithfully an intent gets carried out. If the problem sits in the subject or the verb, meaning nobody holds the intent, then better fidelity won't help. Your manager is like that: he has no intent to *collect* what his employees tell him, so there's nothing for Elephant-2000 machinery to carry. If the intent is there but carried badly or slowly, tooling can help. Most real cases will be mixed. The test is still useful because it tells you which part of a client's problem you can actually take on.

㊢ ("fitted to the PBASE and R-number outlines") The verbs already map onto PBASE through `xiaoxiang-mark-keys`. Against the R-nodes, my first reading (not yet checked against the Lean spec) is:

| verb | R-node |
|---|---|
| delegate | R10 |
| verify by a second process | R9 (no self-certification) |
| constrain responses to calibrated answers | R12 |
| constrain spend | R11 (shared budget) |
| defer | R16 |
| report-problem on regressions | R20 (tripwires) |
| prioritize | R19, the preference C-vector |

R19 is set by people, so in War Machine terms that's where the human-problem boundary sits. One thing surprised me. The three *constrain* rows where FUTON has no tool (typed answers, access scope, spending limit) fall on R11 and R12. So the War Machine already specifies them even though the stack doesn't implement them.

㊟ ("actual customer or client problems") Some of this work already exists. `M-joe-told-me-about-futon` §2c collected public pain signals in six clusters, but they're nearly all *developer* pain: context loss, drift, review load, cost. A company in middle America turning to AI is a different population, and nobody has looked at it yet.

㊭ (next, if you want it) I could do that pass. I'd collect a dozen concrete problems that non-tech organisations say they're bringing AI to, such as intake, scheduling, compliance paperwork and customer follow-up, and write each one as triples. Then I'd sort each problem into human, tooling, or mixed. That would show which verbs come up in real demand, which was your question about why some verbs are more interesting than others.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text: (gist) The draft is in the mission as §3, "DERIVE (draft): operator intents as SVO", committed and pushed as `abf6171`. It has six rules and 20 triples built from GLOSS, plus a short list of verbs the 象 set is missing.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text:
(the rules) The subject is always the operator. The verb has to be one of the 21 象 intents, and any verb that isn't goes on the gap list rather than being invented in the row. Each row then gives:
- the **object**
- the **actions** the tool performs, described mechanically
- the **vendor words**, kept only so you can look a name up
- the FUTON counterpart
- a **fidelity check**: how you'd know the action carried out the intent

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text: ("delegate the act of paying") Row 18 is *delegate · payment*, via "spend from a funded wallet up to a limit". The check is that spending stays within the limit and each purchase traces back to a task. That leaves nothing for an opinion to attach to. Payment is the object, so **pay** doesn't need to be a verb. The only real gap so far is **compare** (Braintrust's A-vs-B), which *explore* doesn't capture.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text: (what the draft shows) Ten of the tools fall under *delegate* or *verify*, which is where most of the selling is. The three rows with no FUTON counterpart (3 typed answers, 8 access scope, 18 spending limit) are all *constrain*. Rule 1 also removes the vendor words without losing anything. "The agent decides / learns / steers" only ever filled the subject slot.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text: (open) Rows 14 and 19 are the shakiest. In row 14 I made the operator's intent *collect/explore* run events, because the stream is something the operator wants to watch, not something the agent "reports". In row 19, p2r has every participant report their own work, agents included. So it may be the one tool that breaks rule 1, or it may just be a schema.
